title: A toy poker game
objectives: Find the best bluffing and calling frequencies in a three-card poker game.

screens.title: Calling a bluffer
screens.prose: Last bet of a hand: Ana bets £100 into a £100 pot. Ben's hand beats only her bluffs. Calling wins £200 against a bluff and loses £100 against a value bet. Slide the share of Ana's bets that are bluffs.

params.xLabel: Share of Ana's bets that are bluffs

derive.caption: If {{fixed(100 * x0, 0)}}% of bets are bluffs, Ben's call earns {{fixed(300 * x0 - 100, 2)}} pounds.

controls.label: Share of bets that are bluffs

screens.question: At what bluff share does Ben not care whether he calls?

feedback.correct: $\tfrac13$: one bluff for every two value bets.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide until Ben's call earns £0.

byKey.half: At one half, Ben's call earns £50, so he should always call.
byKey.quarter: A quarter is the price of a call against a half-pot bet. This bet is pot-sized.

explain.text: Ben's call earns $200x - 100(1 - x) = 300x - 100$, zero at $x = \tfrac13$. If Ana bluffs that often, calling and folding pay Ben the same. That is the bluff share that leaves Ben nothing to exploit.

screens.title: How often Ben calls
screens.prose: Turn it round. A bluff risks Ana's £100 to win the £100 pot. Ben calls a fraction c of the time.
screens.question: How often must Ben call so that Ana's bluffs break even?

hints.text: A bluff wins £100 when Ben folds and loses £100 when he calls.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set Ana's bluff to break even.

byKey.third: A third is Ana's bluff share. Ben's calling frequency comes from her bluff's risk and reward.
byKey.always: Calling always makes bluffs lose, but then Ana stops bluffing and Ben pays off her value bets.

explain.text: A bluff earns $100(1 - c) - 100c$, zero at $c = \tfrac12$. So Ben calls half the time and Ana bluffs a third of her bets. Each player's mix makes the other indifferent, as in lesson 4.

screens.title: A half-pot bet
screens.prose: Now Ana bets £50 into £100. Ben's call risks £50 to win £150; Ana's bluff risks £50 to win £100.

params.xLabel: Share of Ana's bets that are bluffs

screens.question: Fill in Ana's bluff share and Ben's calling frequency.

rows: Share of Ana's bets that are bluffs

feedback.correct: $\tfrac14$ of bets are bluffs and Ben calls $\tfrac23$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Make each player's action break even for the other.

byKey.r0c1: Ben's call breaks even when $150x = 50(1 - x)$: $x = \tfrac14$.
byKey.r1c1: Ana's bluff breaks even when $100(1 - c) = 50c$: $c = \tfrac23$.

explain.text: One bluff for three value bets, $\tfrac{50}{200} = \tfrac14$, and Ben calls $\tfrac{100}{150} = \tfrac23$. The bluff share equals the caller's price from lesson 11, 25%. A smaller bet needs fewer bluffs and more calls.

screens.title: Three cards
screens.prose: Kuhn's three-card poker, cut down: a jack, a queen and a king. Each player antes £1 and gets one card. Ana may bet £1 or check; a check goes straight to showdown. Facing a bet, Ben calls or folds.
screens.question: Fill in the equilibrium frequencies.

hints.text: The king always wins and the jack never does; the queen is in between.
Ana's jack bluffs make Ben's queen indifferent; Ben's queen calls make Ana's jack indifferent.

feedback.correct: King always, jack a third; Ben's queen calls a third, his jack never.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Make Ben's queen indifferent, then Ana's jack.

byKey.r1c1: Facing a bet, Ben's queen wins £3 against a jack and loses £1 to a king. Indifference needs one jack bet per three kings: $\tfrac13$.
byKey.r2c1: Checking the jack loses £1. Bluffing gains £2 on that when Ben folds and loses £1 more when he calls. So Ben calls $\tfrac23$ of bets: every king and a third of his queens.
byKey.r3c1: Ben's jack loses to every bet, so he never calls with it.

explain.text: Ana bets every king and one jack in three, and checks the queen. Ben calls with the king, folds the jack and calls with the queen one time in three. The game is worth $+£\tfrac{1}{18}$, 5.6p a hand, to Ana, who alone can bet.

screens.title: Bet a sure loser
screens.prose: In the three-card game, Ana's jack never wins at showdown.
screens.question: How often should Ana bet the jack?

options.text: Never: a bluff loses when called
options.why: If Ana never bluffs, Ben folds every queen to her bets and her kings win only the antes.

options.text: Half the time, to be unpredictable
options.why: Half is too often: Ben's queen would call every time and win.
Always bluffing lets Ben call every bet with his queen.

hints.text: What does Ben do with his queen if Ana never bluffs?
He folds it to every bet, so her kings win little.
Bluffing a third of her jacks keeps his queen indifferent.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what Ben does against each bluffing rate.

byKey.b: If Ana never bluffs, Ben folds every queen to her bets and her kings win only the antes.

explain.text: A bluff that loses when called still pays if it makes Ben pay off her kings. At one jack in three, Ben's queen is indifferent. Never bluffing is as readable as always bluffing.

screens.title: An unbalanced bettor
screens.prose: Back to the pot-sized bet: Ana bets £100 into £100. Suppose she bluffs more than a third of her bets.

params.xLabel: Share of Ana's bets that are bluffs

screens.question: What should Ben do?

options.text: Call half the time, as at equilibrium
options.why: Half is right only when Ana is balanced. With more bluffs, each call earns more than £0.
Folding is right when she bluffs less than a third. Here she bluffs more.

hints.text: Read the line to the right of $\tfrac13$.
Ben's call earns more than £0 there.

feedback.correct: Call every time: each call earns more than £0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the sign of Ben's call to the right of a third.

byKey.b: Half is right only when Ana is balanced. With more bluffs, each call earns more than £0.

explain.text: With more than a third bluffs, Ben's call earns $300x - 100 > 0$, so he calls everything. With fewer, he folds everything. An unbalanced player is exploited by a pure reply.

screens.title: Bluff and defend
screens.prose:
On the last bet, for a bet $B$ into a pot $P$:

$$\text{bluffs} = \frac{B}{P + 2B} \text{ of bets}, \qquad \text{calls} = \frac{P}{P + B} \text{ of the time}$$

The bettor makes the caller indifferent; the caller makes the bluff indifferent.
screens.question: Ana bets £150 into £100. What share of her bets should be bluffs?

options.why: That is $\tfrac{B}{P + B}$: it leaves Ben's call out of the final pot.
That is Ben's calling frequency, $\tfrac{P}{P + B}$, not the bluff share.
A third is the pot-sized answer. A bigger bet needs more bluffs.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $B = 150$ and $P = 100$ into $\tfrac{B}{P + 2B}$.

explain.text: Ben's call risks £150 to win £250, so it breaks even at $\tfrac{150}{400} = \tfrac38$ bluffs. Bigger bets carry more bluffs and get fewer calls. Ben calls $\tfrac{100}{250} = \tfrac25$ of the time.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Three spots, about two minutes each, as a senior trader would ask them. Say the reasoning aloud before you answer. Give fractions or decimals.
screens.question: Fill in the five answers.

rows: £200 into £100: share of bets that are bluffs
£200 into £100: how often the caller calls
£75 into £100: share of bets that are bluffs
£75 into £100: how often the caller calls
Three-card game: Ana also bets every queen, still bluffs the jack a third, Ben replies best. Her value (£)

hints.text: A betting queen is called by kings and folded by jacks.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r4c1: A betting queen is called by kings and folded by jacks: it loses £2 or wins £1. Ben's queen is then indifferent, and either reply gives Ana $-\tfrac19$, down from $+\tfrac{1}{18}$.

explain.text: Twice the pot: $\tfrac{200}{500} = \tfrac25$ bluffs and $\tfrac{100}{300} = \tfrac13$ calls. £75: $\tfrac{75}{250} = \tfrac{3}{10}$ and $\tfrac{100}{175} = \tfrac47$. A betting queen gets called only when beaten, so Ana's value falls to $-£\tfrac19$.

screens.title: Follow-up: both can bet
screens.prose: The interviewer lets Ben bet £1 too after Ana checks; Ana may then call or fold. This is the full three-card game. Do not derive the equilibrium: state its value and check it.
screens.question: What is the full game worth to Ana, who acts first, in £ a hand?

hints.text: Acting first now gives Ben information before he bets.
The known value is minus one eighteenth.

feedback.correct: $-£\tfrac{1}{18}$: acting first is now a cost.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask who gains once Ben can bet after a check.

byKey.plus: $+\tfrac{1}{18}$ was the cut-down game, where only Ana could bet. Now Ben acts last and gains.
byKey.zero: The game is not fair: the player who acts second wins about 5.6p a hand.

explain.text: The full game is worth $-£\tfrac{1}{18}$ to the first player. Best replies over all 64 pure plans on each side confirm it. A maker who always quotes the same size is as easy to read as a player who never bluffs.

ideas: On the last bet, bluff just often enough that a call breaks even: $\tfrac{B}{P + 2B}$ of bets.
Call just often enough that a bluff breaks even: $\tfrac{P}{P + B}$ of the time.
A player who bluffs too often or too rarely is beaten by always calling or always folding.
summary.trap: Never bluffing, because bluffs lose when called. Then the caller folds and your value bets earn nothing.

quiz.prose: On the last bet Ana bets £100 into a £300 pot.
quiz.question: What share of her bets should be bluffs?

byKey.third: A third fits a pot-sized bet. This bet is a third of the pot.
byKey.quarter: $\tfrac{100}{400}$ leaves the caller's own £100 out of the final pot.

explain.text: The caller risks £100 to win £400, so he breaks even at $\tfrac{100}{500} = \tfrac15$ bluffs. That is Ana's bluff share.

quiz.question: How often should the caller call?

byKey.half: Half fits a pot-sized bet. A small bet must be called more often.

explain.text: Ana's bluff risks £100 to win £300, so it breaks even when Ben calls $\tfrac{300}{400} = \tfrac34$ of the time.

quiz.prose: An opponent has never bluffed in a thousand hands. He bets the river and you hold a hand that beats only bluffs.
quiz.question: What do you do?

options.why: Calling half the time is the reply to a balanced bettor. Against no bluffs every call loses.
Your hand beats only bluffs, and he has none.

feedback.correct: Fold: against no bluffs, every call loses.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what your call beats.

explain.text: Your hand beats only bluffs, and this player never bluffs. Every call loses the bet. An unbalanced player is exploited by a pure reply.
